Salut, c’est Christelle !\n\nÉtant moi-m:
Hi, it’s Christelle!

Being a musician myself, I never heard of Black classical musicians throughout my entire childhood. When I finally did, I was in my twenties and had long since left classical music behind for other genres. My former music teacher, who had taught me when I was younger, organized opera events for up-and-coming opera singers. At one of these events, I met Chantale Nurse, who that night had won every top prize. Her mother, who was there, confided in me how being the only Black person in that environment could create a feeling of loneliness. Since then, I’ve come to appreciate opera. So I can imagine the effect the Obiora Ensemble has on listeners from all walks of life.
« Je suis d’origine martiniquaise, la mu: “I’m of Martinican descent, and music has always been part of my culture. It was more zouk and French pop at home, so nothing to do with classical music!” says Allison Migeon, co-founder of the Obiora Ensemble, about her childhood. Her first encounter with classical music came through ballet. Later, as an adult, she wanted to work in the field, becoming an arts administrator.
Allison s’est installée à Montréal il y: Allison settled in Montréal almost seven years ago. “Once I was here, I said to myself: Oh! No way am I going back to France!” she says, laughing. Over there, she studied at a school specializing in performing arts, before working for various orchestras, ensembles, festivals and production companies. The arts administrator regrets that these schools are not accessible, given the cost and the requirements to get in. “I really struggled to find my place,” she says of the French professional scene. In Montréal, she managed to create her own, and she helps promote the places of others with Obiora, a classical music ensemble she co-founded in 2021 with her partner, double bassist Brandyn Lewis.
Obiora est composé de musiciens professi: Obiora is made up of professional musicians, most of them from culturally diverse backgrounds. Its goal: to promote and increase the representation of different cultural backgrounds in classical music.
L’idée d’un tel projet prend forme en 20: The idea for such a project took shape in 2020, in the middle of the pandemic. “Like a lot of people, it was a moment to pause and reflect,” Allison recalls. Many equity, diversity and inclusion policies were being put in place at that time, in a context heightened by the death of George Floyd. “People were starting to ask questions. We asked ourselves those same questions: what place is there for the representation of people of different origins in classical music?”
Allison Migeon, co-fondatrice de l’Ensem: Allison Migeon, co-founder of the Obiora Ensemble Photographer Miet Verhauwaert
Son conjoint Brandyn Lewis, directeur ar: Her partner Brandyn Lewis, Obiora’s artistic director and a double bassist with the Montreal Symphony Orchestra, the National Arts Centre Orchestra in Ottawa and the Quebec Symphony Orchestra, has often been the only Black musician in those institutions. “We really asked ourselves: how is that possible?” Allison recalls.
Tanya Charles, violoniste noire basée à: Tanya Charles, a Black violinist based in Toronto, was living the same situation and sharing the same thoughts. “When we told her about our project, she was immediately on board,” says Allison. The project quickly took shape, carried by the enthusiasm of musicians who wanted to contribute. “Right away, it took off with incredible momentum. Everyone was super happy to be part of the adventure. That’s how it came about.”
Au début, l’idée est de se regrouper ent: At first, the idea was to bring together friends and people with the same interests. “We realized it met a real need, both for artists and for audiences.”
Pas moins de 200 personnes assistent au: No fewer than 200 people attended Obiora’s first concert in August 2021. “Of the four works presented at that concert, three were by composers of African descent that nobody had ever heard of. And it didn’t deter people from coming at all.”
Obiora est aujourd’hui un organisme à bu: Obiora is now a non-profit organization and a registered charity. “We wanted to put on concerts, but we also wanted to have an impact on the community,” says Allison.
Les fondateurs d’Obiara veulent rendre l: Obiora’s founders want to make classical music accessible to everyone, so that everyone feels welcome. “Unfortunately, there are still too many prejudices about this world. People still feel it’s too elitist,” laments the executive director. The organization therefore offers music workshops for children and adults “for people in general who don’t go to concerts or don’t know classical music.” “We realized there’s a real need, a real demand.”
Le public, plus familier avec le milieu: The audience, more familiar with the classical music world, is surprised by the diversity of the crowd in terms of cultural backgrounds, ages and occupations. “We really have an audience that’s very different from what you usually see in a concert hall. And that was our goal,” says Allison, delighted.
L’an dernier, lors du premier concert de: Last year, at the first concert of the season, Obiora performed a violin concerto by Florence Price (1887-1953). She was the first African American woman symphonic composer, and her legacy includes more than 300 works. Tanya Charles, the ensemble’s first violin, was the soloist. “There were people crying in the audience!” says Allison. “Several Black women came up to us and said: ‘It’s the first time we’ve seen a Black woman showcased like that, with an orchestra,’” Allison says.
La directrice générale croit à la force: The executive director believes in the power of representation. “People tell us: I played music when I was young, but since nobody looked like me, I couldn’t even see myself continuing. I never thought of becoming a professional musician.”
Allison Migeon souhaite faire comprendre: Allison Migeon wants parents to understand that professional opportunities are possible. “For [parents], making music isn’t a potential career,” she laments. She remembers a young Black double bassist who, after seeing Brandyn play on stage, told him: “I play double bass, and one day I’m going to play with Obiora!”
Obiora n’a pas l’ambition de devenir un: Obiora has no ambition to become a symphony orchestra and wants to keep its community mission. “In our approach, we make ourselves available after concerts.” That’s the watchword for the musicians: take the time to go meet the audience. “Because people need (...) to communicate, to express their emotions.”
L’absence de diversité dans le milieu es: The lack of diversity in the field is so glaring that professional musicians themselves come to believe there simply aren’t any other racialized musicians, Allison explains. “But that’s false,” she says. What explains such an absence? Several barriers, economic ones in particular, stand in the way of young people from various cultural communities. “The more you think about it, the more you realize there’s also a problem of access to music. It should be free and accessible to everyone, and it really isn’t. It remains an expensive discipline: you have to take lessons, buy or rent an instrument. It takes a lot of discipline, a lot of time.”
Obiora is therefore trying to change the game. As a pilot project, the organization set up a twenty-week violin program in a public school in Saint-Michel. Every week, teachers give violin lessons to the children, and each student has their own instrument.
Les cours viennent de prendre fin et le: The classes have just ended, and the project couldn’t meet the demand. “We had forty spots in our program and more than a hundred students wanted to sign up,” says Allison. “[Adults] have prejudices, they think [children] won’t be interested. But no, when you give them access, there’s interest.”
Il n’est pas rare que des enfants n’aien: It’s not uncommon for children to have no music education at school or at home, Allison notes. “The goal isn’t necessarily to turn them into professional musicians, but to give them a little spark, so they discover something new,” she explains.
Par la suite, si un enfant a envie de po: Afterwards, if a child wants to keep learning an instrument, it’s possible to go on to a high school with a music program. “It’s essential to tell yourself that it opens up a world for them, one more door.”

La directrice d’Obiora pense qu’une tell: Obiora’s director thinks such an initiative on the other side of the Atlantic would have come with a different set of challenges. “To be ‘well integrated’ in French society, you have to assimilate. Obiora’s project would be seen there as communitarianism,” she believes. She gives the example of Zahia Ziouani, a French conductor of Algerian descent. “She created her own orchestra. She’s a woman of North African descent who grew up in the Paris suburbs in the ’80s,” she explains. “She faced both misogyny and racism along the way. But when I see how the French media talk about her, very often they emphasize the fact that she’s a woman. They never mention her origins or the fact that she grew up in the suburbs.”
Un tout autre son de métronome résonne a: A completely different metronome is ticking in the United States. Allison Migeon took part in <l1>SphinxConnect</l1>, a summit on diversity and inclusion in classical music, in Detroit last January. There, the worry was palpable, particularly over the cancellation of diversity initiatives imposed by the Trump administration. “The general feeling is that we have to find strategies to keep doing the work, even if it means adapting the language and the labels to get around resistance,” Allison notes.
Sur les 2200 personnes présentes sur pla: Of the 2,200 people in attendance, Allison saw few Canadian institutions, and none from Quebec, whereas major American orchestras and schools such as Berklee College of Music and Juilliard were there. “I noticed that a lot of white people from the United States come to this kind of event because they want to understand what the issues are, how their colleagues feel, how the people they invite feel. And I don’t get the impression we’re there yet in Canada.”
Il faut dire qu’aux États-Unis, la musiq: It must be said that in the United States, music is more accessible. An incalculable number of professional musicians come from public music schools and programs. “There are specific programs, dedicated foundations that fund them. Opportunities that simply don’t exist in Canada,” says the ensemble’s executive director. Obiora drew particular inspiration from the Chineke! Orchestra in London, which promotes the professional paths of musicians of different backgrounds. “What’s happening in Canada? Does it exist? How is it that a country like Canada is so far behind?”
Elle relève tout de même les efforts de: She nonetheless points to the efforts of major Quebec institutions when it comes to diversity. “A conductor like Rafael Payare, I think, really breathed new life into programming. Same for the Orchestre Métropolitain with Yannick Nézet-Séguin. He’s someone who has always shown an interest in diversity, who really tries to build bridges.”
Elle applaudit aussi le programme El Sis: She also applauds the Montreal Symphony Orchestra’s El Sistema program, which has just been launched and gives 600 students the opportunity to play in a youth orchestra. “I think this type of initiative has to continue. It’s really what can make the difference, letting these young people keep learning their instrument, pursue their studies, then find themselves in a position to audition and maybe join orchestras,” she explains.
Car il est bien là, le problème. Ce n’es: Because that’s where the problem really lies. It’s not that orchestras resist diversifying their personnel, it’s that musicians have to audition, Allison explains. At this stage, very few of them come from diverse backgrounds. “If, out of fifty people who come to audition, there’s one Black person, one Latino person, one South Asian person, and those three don’t make it past the first round, inevitably, in the end, there will only be white people left.”
C’est précisément pour cette raison que: That’s precisely why Obiora’s audition criteria are different. “We give priority to people from culturally diverse backgrounds, because we know they have fewer opportunities,” says Ms. Migeon. It’s not at all about lowering the standards of excellence; Obiora remains a group of professional musicians. “We can’t take everyone. Also, let’s not kid ourselves, we’re up against prejudices toward people from diverse backgrounds, who aren’t considered professional,” she laments.
L’Ensemble Obiora, avec le contre-bassis: The Obiora Ensemble, with double bassist and co-founder Brandyn Lewis - Photographer Tam Photography
Obiora se produit dans des lieux très di: Obiora performs in very different venues. Last fall, the group presented a series of five concerts in CHSLDs (long-term care homes), with a program of composers of African descent. For the group, it’s just routine, but for the audience, it’s anything but.
Les commentaires positifs ont fusé. « De: The positive comments poured in. “Ladies would come up to us and exclaim: ‘Oh, I didn’t know these composers at all, it’s incredible! It’s so good, it’s so beautiful! You gave us a lovely time…’ Well, that’s what we want!” says Allison.
Obiora mise aussi sur l’accessibilité. «: Obiora also bets on accessibility. “We chose to set extremely low prices, compared to what’s usually done. Most people today, especially with inflation and everything, can’t put $85 per person toward going to a concert.”
Pour établir le prix des concerts, Mme M: To set concert prices, Ms. Migeon polled friends, young people and students who aren’t in the classical music field. “We told them: you who don’t listen to classical music in general, how much money would you pay to see our concert, or any other concert?” As a result, concert tickets cost $30, and $20 for students. For children, it’s free. “We said to ourselves: what’s the point of parents coming if they don’t bring their kids?!”
Obiora établit également des partenariat: Obiora also forms partnerships with organizations to offer them complimentary tickets, for example organizations that serve new immigrants or that help women in shelters. “We don’t give out tickets to fill our hall. We give tickets because for us, it makes sense to welcome those people who, very often, find themselves in situations where they have no money, no contacts, no network.”
L’initiative vit aussi grâce à des subve: The initiative also lives on government grants and donations. While budget cuts are ravaging the cultural sector, the music world isn’t spared. The Orchestre Métropolitain had to cancel performances, and several others had to cancel concerts or shorten their seasons. Obiora is no exception. “Last year, we had four big concerts and we chose to do two.” Marginalized people are just as short on resources. “People think: ‘Oh, but diversity, it’s so easy for you, you just have to ask and everyone gives you money! It’s so easy for you, because you tick the boxes!’ And no! Not at all!”
Obiora vise à présenter des pièces qui n: Obiora aims to present pieces that have never been played in Quebec, or even in Canada. The last concert of the season was held this Sunday, May 11, at Salle Pierre-Mercure in the Centre Pierre-Péladeau. It featured Jaelem Bhate, conductor of the Prince Edward Island Symphony Orchestra, and welcomed pianist John Kofi Dapaah, a Canadian of Ghanaian descent, who played Florence Price’s one-movement concerto. Also on the program were the wind quintet by Ted Runcie, a Canadian composer of Jamaican descent, and a piece by Fela Sowande, a Nigerian composer, with music titled African Suite. “I fell in love with this piece when I heard it on the radio on CBC.”
